SNAKE BITE — FIRST AID
What to Do Immediately After a Snake Bite
Snake bite is a serious medical emergency, and India — including rural and semi-urban parts of Odisha — has one of the highest snake bite burdens in the world. Most deaths happen not because a bite is untreatable, but because the person reaches a hospital too late or wastes critical time on harmful home remedies. The steps below reflect current public health guidance and are meant to help people act quickly, calmly, and safely.
What to Do Immediately
Stay calm and keep the person calm. Fear and movement speed up blood circulation, which can spread venom faster. Reassure the person — many snake bites, even from venomous species, do not result in death, and some bites do not inject venom at all.
Move away from the snake. Do not try to catch, kill, or identify it up close. If it is safe to do so from a distance, noting its colour and shape (or a photo) can help doctors, but this should never delay getting help.
Keep the bitten limb still and positioned below the level of the heart, if possible. Immobilize it loosely the way you would a fracture, using a splint or cloth, to reduce movement.
Remove tight items near the bite — rings, bangles, watches, or tight clothing — before swelling begins, since swelling can make these dangerously constricting later.
Gently wash the bite area with clean water if available, without scrubbing or applying anything else to it.
Get the person to the nearest hospital or Primary Health Centre (PHC) as fast as possible. This is the single most important step, since anti-snake venom (ASV) and emergency care can only be given at a health facility.
Call for emergency transport immediately — dial 108 for India's free ambulance service, or arrange the fastest available transport, while continuing to keep the person still and calm en route.
What NOT to Do
Do not cut, slash, or make incisions on or near the bite wound.
Do not try to suck out the venom by mouth or with a suction device.
Do not tie a tight tourniquet or ligature around the limb — this can cut off blood flow and cause serious harm without stopping venom spread.
Do not apply ice, cold packs, or any chemical, herbal paste, or traditional remedy to the wound.
Do not give the person alcohol, tea, coffee, or any food or drink, as this can complicate treatment.
Do not rely on faith healers, mantra treatment, or unproven traditional practices instead of a hospital — these delay real treatment and cost lives.
Do not let the person walk, run, or exert themselves; carry or transport them instead.
Do not waste time trying to catch or kill the snake — hospitals can treat venomous bites using a standard antivenom without needing the exact snake.
When to Call Emergency Services
Treat every suspected venomous snake bite as a medical emergency, even if the person feels fine at first — symptoms of envenoming can appear after a delay. Call for an ambulance (108) or begin transport to the nearest government hospital or PHC/CHC immediately in the following situations:
Any bite from a snake that cannot be confidently identified as harmless.
Swelling, severe pain, or bruising that spreads from the bite site.
Bleeding from the gums, nose, or the bite wound itself, or blood in urine.
Drooping eyelids, blurred vision, difficulty speaking or swallowing, or slurred speech.
Difficulty breathing, chest tightness, or weakness in the limbs.
Nausea, vomiting, dizziness, or fainting.
Government hospitals under Odisha's health system and the National Health Mission are expected to stock free polyvalent anti-snake venom (ASV) for treating bites from the country's major venomous species. Do not wait at home to “see if symptoms appear” — early hospital arrival gives the best chance of full recovery.
Source Basis
This content is based on general, publicly available guidance from recognised health authorities, paraphrased and adapted for awareness purposes. It does not quote any source directly. Reference sources consulted:
World Health Organization (WHO) — Guidelines for the Management of Snakebites and the WHO snakebite envenoming topic page
Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India — National Snakebite Management Protocol and Standard Treatment Guidelines for Snakebite Management
National Health Mission (NHM), India — National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (NAPSE)
Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) — published research on snakebite burden and management in India
Mayo Clinic — general public first-aid guidance on snake bites
This content is for general awareness only and does not replace professional medical advice.
